# Citations and Grounding {.unnumbered}

## Why This Matters

Reports can sound confident even when claims are weakly supported. A grounding audit forces each important claim to point back to a source: code output, a table, a figure, a citation, or a stated limitation.

## Citation Workflow

The course uses BibTeX references through `references.bib`. A report YAML header can include:

```yaml
---
title: "Project Report"
format: html
bibliography: ../../references.bib
---
```

Then cite a source in text:

```markdown
The NHANES classroom example is derived from CDC/NCHS NHANES public-use data [@cdc-nhanes].
```

If your project uses a different source, add the relevant bibliography entry to the report's local `references.bib` or to the project bibliography.

## Grounding Audit

For A9, choose at least three claims and trace them.

| Claim | Evidence type | Evidence location | Decision |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mean BMI differs by income group. | Figure/table | Results plot and summary table | Keep, with descriptive wording |
| Income causes BMI differences. | None | Not supported | Remove or rewrite |
| The summary is unweighted. | Methods/code | Methods paragraph and code | Keep |

## What Counts as Evidence

Evidence can be:

- a code-generated table;
- a code-generated figure;
- a data source citation;
- a methods paragraph;
- a limitation statement;
- a reproducibility log.

Evidence is not:

- an AI-generated sentence without verification;
- a visual impression with no source;
- a claim copied from a website without citation;
- a dashboard interaction that cannot be reproduced.

## AI-Use Check

If AI helped draft report prose, audit the generated text for:

- invented sources;
- stronger claims than the code supports;
- causal language;
- missing limitations;
- mismatched variable names or statistics.

## Before Moving On

If a claim cannot be grounded, do one of three things:

- add the missing evidence;
- soften the wording;
- remove the claim.
